name: Sports Management Marketing
objectives: Given a real or planned sports event, write a one-sentence offer and name the audience who decides to come or pay, with date, place, cost and approvals confirmed with your athletic director or league

Using your offer and an AI assistant, write a one-page promotion plan with channels, one main message and a timeline, with three to five channels, an announce, remind, last-week and thank-you timeline, and a person assigned to each task
Using an AI assistant and a Canva template, create a flyer and a social post with the five event facts, proofread by someone else and following your school's rules on logos and photos of minors

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What you are offering and to whom
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-sentence offer and audience for your event.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real or planned sports event, you will write a one-sentence offer and name the audience who decides to come or pay, with date, place, cost and approvals confirmed with your athletic director or league.
Every event is an offer: something people get in return for their time or money. A youth camp offers skills and fun in a safe place. A home game offers entertainment and community. A tournament offers competition for teams.
Write your offer in one sentence: "A two-day beginner soccer camp for kids aged 6 to 10, run by our varsity players, with a T-shirt and snacks, on June 12-13." Then name the audience: who decides to come or pay? For a youth camp, that is the parents.
Before you market anything, confirm the basics with your athletic director or league: date, place, cost, insurance, safety and any approval needed.
Step by step:
- Name the event.
- Write what people get.
- Name who decides to come or pay.
- Confirm date, place, cost and approvals with your athletic director or league.
Words to know:
- Offer: what people get in return for their time or money.
- Athletic director: the person who runs a school's sports program and approves events.
Try it now: Pick a real or planned event. Write its one-sentence offer and name the audience who decides to come or pay.
You can now describe an event's offer and its deciding audience in one sentence.

check.q: What does a home game offer the people who come?
check.why: Every event is an offer; a home game offers entertainment and community.

check.q: You want to run a tournament next month. What do you do before any marketing?
options: Post the date on social media
Confirm date, place, cost, insurance and approvals with your athletic director or league
check.why: Confirm the basics and approvals before you market anything.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The one-page promotion plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page plan with channels, messages and a timeline.
This lesson builds toward: Using your offer and an AI assistant, you will write a one-page promotion plan with channels, one main message and a timeline, with three to five channels, an announce, remind, last-week and thank-you timeline, and a person assigned to each task.
A promotion plan answers: where will the audience hear about it, what will we say, and when? Keep it to one page.
Local sports events often do best with a mix: school or club newsletters, the team's social accounts, local Facebook groups, flyers at schools, gyms and stores, word of mouth from players and families, and local news or community calendars.
Use a simple timeline: announce about four to six weeks before, remind two weeks before, push hard the last week, and post thank-yous after. An AI assistant can turn your notes into a clean table.
Step by step:
- List three to five channels.
- Write one main message.
- Make a timeline: announce, remind, last week, thank-you.
- Ask AI to put it into a one-page table.
- Assign who does each task.
Words to know:
- Promotion: telling people about your event so they come.
- Timeline: what happens on which dates.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant: "Turn these notes into a one-page promotion plan table with channel, message, date and who is responsible." Paste your event notes and edit the result.
You can now write a one-page promotion plan with channels, a message, a timeline and owners.

check.q: What three questions does a promotion plan answer?
options: Who plays, who wins, who scores
Where the audience hears about it, what we say, and when
How much, how long, how far
Which logo, which color, which font
check.why: A promotion plan covers channels, message and timing.

check.q: Your event is next week and nobody is assigned to post reminders. What do you do?
options: Assign a person to each promotion task now
check.why: Each task in the plan needs a person responsible.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Making promo materials with AI and Canva
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a flyer and a social post for your event that follow your school's rules.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant and a Canva template, you will create a flyer and a social post with the five event facts, proofread by someone else and following your school's rules on logos and photos of minors.
Every promo piece needs the same five facts: what, who it's for, when, where, and how to sign up or get tickets. Add one photo and one reason to come.
Use an AI assistant to draft short wording, then use a free design tool like Canva to build a flyer and a square social post from a template.
Follow your school or league rules on logos, team names and photos of minors. Use photos only with permission, and many schools require a media release from parents before posting photos of students.
Step by step:
- List the five facts.
- Ask AI for a headline and two short lines.
- Build a flyer and a social post in Canva.
- Check logos and photos against your school's rules.
- Have someone else proofread the date, time and link.
Words to know:
- Media release: a signed permission to use someone's photo or video.
- Proofread: check carefully for mistakes before sharing.
Try it now: Make a flyer and a social post for your event. Ask someone else to check the five facts and the sign-up link.
You can now make clear promo materials that follow school and photo rules.

check.q: Which of these is one of the five facts every promo piece needs?
options: How to sign up or get tickets
check.why: What, who it's for, when, where and how to sign up go on every piece.

check.q: Your flyer is finished. What do you do before sharing it?
options: Add more photos of students without asking
Have someone else proofread the date, time and link
check.why: Another person catches mistakes in the key details.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building a local sponsor package
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a three-level sponsor package a local business can say yes to.
This lesson builds toward: Given what your school allows you to offer, you will build a three-level local sponsor package, with prices checked with your athletic director, only promises you can deliver, and money routed through the official process.
A sponsor is a business that gives money, products or services in return for being seen by your audience. Local businesses like pizza shops, car dealers, gyms and dentists often sponsor school and club sports.
Make it easy with three levels, for example Bronze, Silver and Gold. Each level lists what the sponsor gives and what they get: name on the banner, logo on the T-shirt, a social post thanking them, announcements at games, or a table at the event. Only promise what you can deliver and what your school allows.
Set prices by asking your athletic director what other sponsors have paid and what your costs are. Do not guess big numbers, and keep the money handling within your school or club's official process.
Step by step:
- List what you can offer sponsors that your school allows.
- Group the offers into three levels.
- Ask your athletic director about past prices and your costs.
- Put the package on one page.
- Route money through the official school or club process.
Words to know:
- Sponsor: a business that supports your event in return for being seen.
- Sponsor package: a one-page list of sponsor levels, what they give and what they get.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to help you lay out a three-level sponsor package for your event using only the benefits you listed. Fill in prices only after talking to your athletic director.
You can now build a three-level local sponsor package with clear give-and-get.

options: A business that gives money, products or services to be seen by your audience
check.why: Sponsors give support in return for being seen by your audience.

check.q: A sponsor asks you to put their logo on players' jerseys, but your school does not allow it. What do you do?
options: Do it without telling the school
Offer only what your school allows, such as a banner or a thank-you post
check.why: Only promise what you can deliver and what your school allows.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Pitching a sponsor with an AI-drafted email
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write and send a short, personal sponsor pitch email.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI draft, you will write a sponsor pitch email to one local business, under 150 words, with a true, specific reason you chose them, sent from an official account with one follow-up.
A pitch email is short and personal. It says who you are, what the event is, why their business fits, what you are asking for, and how they benefit. Attach or link the one-page package.
Ask an AI assistant: "Write a short, friendly email to [business type] asking them to sponsor our youth basketball camp. Mention our audience of 80 local families and our Silver level. Under 150 words." Then edit it: add something true and specific about that business and why you chose them.
Follow up once after about a week if you hear nothing. Visiting in person with a player or parent often works better than email for local businesses. Always say thank you, even if they say no.
Step by step:
- Pick one local business that fits your audience.
- Ask AI for a short draft under 150 words.
- Add a true, specific reason you chose them.
- Attach the package and send from an official account.
- Follow up once after a week; thank them either way.
Words to know:
- Pitch: a short request that explains what you want and why it helps them.
- Follow-up: a polite second message if you have not heard back.
Try it now: Choose one local business. Use AI to draft a pitch email, personalize it, and have your coach or athletic director read it before you send it.
You can now write a short, personal sponsor pitch email and follow up politely.

check.q: What should a pitch email include?
options: Who you are, the event, why their business fits, the ask and how they benefit
A long history of the team
check.why: A short, personal pitch covers those five points and links the package.

check.q: A local pizza shop has not answered your pitch after a week. What do you do?
options: Follow up once, or visit with a player or parent
Give up and never ask again
check.why: Follow up once after about a week; visiting in person often works better.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reporting results so sponsors return
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Track event numbers and send sponsors a short thank-you report.
This lesson builds toward: After your event, you will create a one-page sponsor thank-you report with three numbers, a photo and a quote, with every number checked and the report sent within two weeks.
Sponsors come back when they see what they got. Track a few numbers during and after the event: attendance or sign-ups, social post reach and engagement, and anything sponsor-specific like coupon uses or table visits.
Send a one-page thank-you report within two weeks: a photo of their banner or logo at the event, the numbers, a quote from a family or player, and a thank-you from the team.
Ask an AI assistant to turn your numbers and notes into a friendly report, then check every number yourself. Never inflate numbers; trust is what brings sponsors back next year.
Step by step:
- Choose three numbers before the event.
- Collect them during and after.
- Take photos of sponsor signage.
- Draft a one-page report with AI.
- Check every number and send within two weeks.
Words to know:
- Reach: how many people saw a post.
- Thank-you report: a short summary for sponsors with photos and results.
Try it now: Final task: for your event, finish the promotion plan, sponsor package and pitch email, get approval from your athletic director or league, and write the three numbers you will report to sponsors.
You can now report honest results to sponsors so they want to return.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Promotion plan No timeline, too few channels, or no one assigned to tasks. One page with three to five channels, one main message, an announce-remind-last-week-thank-you timeline and an owner for each task. Channels are matched to the deciding audience named in the offer. Sponsor package Fewer than three levels, guessed prices, or promises the school does not allow. Three levels with clear give and get, prices checked with the athletic director, and money through the official process. Each level fits a different size of local business and includes a sponsor-specific number to report. Pitch email Reads as copied AI text, is long, or has no specific reason for that business. Under 150 words, in the writer's own words, with a true reason for choosing the business and the package attached. Includes a follow-up plan and an in-person visit option. Approval and results plan No approval, or no numbers chosen for the sponsor report. Approved by the athletic director or league, with three numbers chosen to report to sponsors. States how each number will be collected and when the report will be sent. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What brings sponsors back the next year?
options: Seeing what they got, with honest numbers
check.why: Sponsors return when a report shows real results.

check.q: AI wrote your report and says 200 people came, but your count was 150. What do you do?
check.why: Check every number yourself and never inflate them.
